text: An algorithm killed more Americans last year than car accidents. Sarah's eight-year-old daughter had approved heart surgery on Tuesday. By Thursday, a computer overruled it. By Sunday, she was dead. Every year, artificial intelligence systems deployed by health insurance companies, automatically deny approximately 1.2 million medical claims that should have been approved. The result isn't just financial hardship. According to internal documents obtained through whistleblowers and court filings, these algorithmic denials directly contribute to an estimated 40,000 preventable deaths annually. That's more Americans killed by corporate algorithms than died in the entire Vietnam War. But unlike Vietnam, this war is happening in hospital rooms across America and the weapons are lines of code designed to maximize shareholder profits by minimizing human survival. The system killing Americans wasn't built by accident. In 2019, United Health Group, a largest health insurer in America, began deploying an AI system called NH predict across their entire claims processing network. The algorithm was trained on millions of historical claims and designed with one primary objective. Reduce the percentage of approved expensive treatments. Internal emails leaked during a 20-23 class action lawsuit, reveal executives celebrating the system's efficiency improvements. What they were really celebrating was a 23% increase in denials for treatments costing more than $10,000. The AI had learned something. Its human program has never explicitly taught it. That poor and sick people are less likely to appeal denied claims. So it began systematically targeting them. But here's what makes this story truly sinister. The AI isn't just denying claims randomly. According to internal training documents, NH predict was designed to identify high risk patients using over 50,000 data points that have nothing to do with medical necessity. The algorithm knows your credit score, your zip code, your shopping habits, and your social media activity. It knows if you've ever filed for bankruptcy, missed a car payment or posted about financial stress. And it uses all of this information to predict one thing. How likely you are to hire a lawyer and fight back? Patients flagged as low litigation risk, typically poor, elderly or non-English speakers, get their expensive treatments denied at rates approaching 90%. The wealthy get approved at nearly the same rate they always did. Dr. Jennifer Walsh discovered the truth by accident. As an emergency room physician at Denver Health, she noticed that patients with identical conditions were getting different insurance responses depending on factors that seemed medically irrelevant. When she started tracking the pattern, she found something chilling. Patients from zip codes with average incomes below $40,000 were $340 more likely to have emergency procedures denied, even when those procedures were identical to ones approved for wealthy patients. Walsh began documenting cases, and what she found was a systematic pattern of algorithmic discrimination that violated both federal anti-discrimination laws and basic medical ethics. Her whistleblower complaint filed with the Department of Health and Human Services includes audio recordings of insurance executives discussing optimization targets and acceptable casualty rates. In one particularly damning recording, a United Health Executive refers to denied patient deaths as statistical normalization. This isn't just happening at United Health. Internal documents from Anthem, Signa and Etna reveal similar AI systems with similar biases. The algorithm that might deny your next medical claim doesn't just look at your diagnosis. It looks at your entire digital footprint to determine your worth as a human being. If your poor, old or vulnerable, the AI has already decided your life isn't worth the cost. And because these decisions happen in milliseconds, most patients never realize they're being systematically discriminated against by machines designed to let them die. Most disturbing part, this is completely legal. Current health care regulations were written decades before AI existed, creating a massive legal loophole that allows insurance companies to deploy discriminatory algorithms with virtually no oversight. While you're fighting for your life, an algorithm is calculating whether your death would be more profitable than your survival. Sarah Martinez never found out exactly why her daughter's surgery was denied after being approved. The algorithm's decision-making process is considered proprietary information protected by trade secrets law. But based on what we now know about these systems, we can make an educated guess. Sarah's family was flagged as unlikely to fight back. They were wrong. Sarah's lawsuit against anthem is now part of a growing movement of families demanding accountability for AI systems that treat human lives as actuarial problems. The question isn't whether these algorithms are killing Americans. The internal documents prove they are. The question is what happens when enough people realize that their insurance companies AI sees them not as patients to heal, but as expenses to eliminate. The documents revealed in this investigation represent just the tip of the iceberg. Next week, we're releasing internal training materials that show exactly how these algorithms determine your litigation risk score. And the simple steps you can take to protect yourself from algorithmic discrimination. Subscribe to get notified when that investigation drops because what you don't know about your insurance company's AI could literally kill you.
